content:
I have a secret to share. The reason this whole series is about “spaces” is just to annoy my dear friend and colleague Dr. Scott Fielder. You see, he was there when computer graphics really started kicking off in the 1980s, and researchers were figuring out how to get 3D models onto the screen efficiently. He used things like the Model-View-Projection matrix, which speeds you through a whole bunch of spaces without blinking. In fact he doesn’t even like the word “spaces”, I mean it’s all just matrix multiplication in the end.

The importance of “spaces” struck me when I became program coordinator for our Game Programming Advanced Diploma at Humber Polytechnic. Part of my duties back then was to organize a program advisory committee full of brilliant people that work in the video game industry, and I would quiz them regularly on what we should be teaching in our program. I asked them often on what they found lacking from new graduates entering the workforce. The lead programmer at a major AAA game studio said new hires typically don’t have a good grasp on “spaces”. I was taken aback. I had thought of spaces at the time as a way to describe certain parts of the rendering pipeline but had never thought it was that important. But since then, I have reflected on all the tricky programming bugs my students had been stuck on when trying to rotate a camera, light a scene, or click on a 3D object. So many logic errors came from doing a calculation in the wrong space or comparing data in totally different spaces.

The term “spaces” seems so vague but there are concrete definitions for the chain of operations needed to get a 3D object from an artist onto your screen. Writing mathematics and code for the right space can save you a huge headache down the line, so I think it is worthwhile exploring these spaces and seeing how to jump between them. Hopefully I’ll convince Scott by the end of this series too :)

I like using the term "Paul Neale" space, rather than model space, as it helps when I’m communicating with Scott. It's easy to get confused when books refer to model space as “object” or “local” space. The rendering process starts with the artist making decisions, so why not go with your favorite artist instead? In fact, I told Paul he is like the multiverse in our program! There is only one world space, but there are infinitely many Paul Neale spaces! Well, not infinite, but every object that Paul creates has its own model space that programmers need to consider when jumping over to world space.

When an artist finishes a 3D model, they click a button in their program to export it as a file. In our Game Programming program, we like handling "OBJ" files. They are simpler than other popular formats, but they are easy to read and a great learning environment for programmers. The OBJ file stores the vertices, normals, and texture coordinates that were created by the artist. When I explain "Paul Neale space” to the man himself, I usually point at an OBJ file as that's where our programmers interface with models. Let's attempt to be a 3D artist by creating a simple square as an OBJ file:


I will break down the shape into two triangles and then identify the vertex positions:


Notice that I have made my first choices as an artist. The square has side lengths of 2, it's centered at the origin, and the shape lies on the x-z plane. These are not earth-shattering decisions, but they will need to be considered by the programmer if they need a larger square in world space or if they need it flat on the x-y plane. Remember that rotations are easy about the origin but take a bit more thinking when rotating about another position. My choice of having the origin at the centre of the square seems reasonable to me, but the programmer will need to live with that decision when rotating the square into world space.

With the model space vertices done, I get to consider the normals. It seems reasonable to have one normal for the entire square pointing along the y direction. If this was a more complicated shape, an artist might have a normal for every vertex to control the look of edges. The GPU interpolates the three vertex normals across a triangle to make a smooth lighting gradient. If an artist wants the appearance of a hard edge, they can specify multiple normals at a single vertex position so that each face corner has its own normal. I have a simple shape, so I can specify one normal for the whole square:


The last vectors that need to be specified in model space are the texture coordinates. If we want to put a 2D image onto a square that lives in 3D, how should it be mapped? The GPU will look at the pixel colors of the picture and then determine which parts of the mesh should be colored as it interpolates across the triangles. The texture axes are called u and v, with u going horizontally and v going vertically. Typically, the bottom left corner has a uv coordinate of (0, 0) and the top right is at (1, 1). This will be easy to set up for my simple square shape, but an artist does more work for a complicated 3D shape. The process of generating the flat uv coordinates from a 3D mesh is called "unwrapping" and as Paul explained it's like flattening out a cardboard box. My square is already flat, so it's easy to set up my texture coordinates:


The last thing we need to do is specify which is the front and the back of the square. It may not seem important when drawing a square on a piece of paper, but the GPU discards any triangles that are facing away from the camera to save work. There is no point rendering the back of someone's head if they are facing the viewer. In the OpenGL graphics library, the convention is to have front facing triangles that are built from a counterclockwise (CCW) set of three vertices. Imagine looking at my square with the normals pointing towards your side of the triangles. Then specify the three vertices for every triangle in a counterclockwise order as they appear to you:


Looking at my scribbles above, you can see the triangle on the left would be specified in the CCW winding order as vertices 1, 2, and 4, or 2, 4, and 1, or even 4, 1, and 2. The triangle on the right would be specified as vertices 2, 3, and 4, or any other order that still goes counterclockwise.

With our vertex positions, normal direction, texture coordinates, and front faces specified, we are now ready to define model space in our own OBJ file. Open a text editor and start typing the vertex positions denoted as "v" with numbers for x, y and z:

v -1 0 1

v 1 0 1

v 1 0 -1

v -1 0 -1

Write the texture coordinates as "vt" with values for the u and v coordinates:

vt 0 0

vt 1 0

vt 1 1

vt 0 1

We only have one normal vector denoted by "vn" with values for x, y, and z:

vn 0 1 0

Finally, specify the vertex information for each triangle corner in the shape. This is denoted as "f" for face and we pick the vertex position, texture coordinate and normal from the list above. Each triangle has three vertices with the numbering for each position, uv coordinate, and normal vector given between "/" symbols in that specific order. So, for example, a vertex that uses the 1st vertex position in the file, the 1st uv coordinate listed, and the 1st (and only) normal vector would be written as "1/1/1":

f 1/1/1 2/2/1 4/4/1

f 2/2/1 3/3/1 4/4/1

Notice that these two triangles follow the CCW winding order in my picture.

Save this work in a file with a ".obj" extension and open it in your favorite 3D viewer to see this:


To see if the texture coordinates work, I used one of my pictures as the texture for the square and placed it in my world space. The GPU takes a look at my scribbles to see what color each pixel of the square shape should be based on the uv coordinates. I made my image a square shape in pixels to ensure it didn't look stretched across the mesh:


Typing out a 3D model is fine for a square, but it quickly gets out of hand with anything more complicated. Try downloading Blender (www.blender.org) or opening your favorite 3D art tool to make something more interesting. Export your model as an OBJ file and compare it to the simple one we built for the square. Then breathe a sigh of relief as we don’t need to type out model space by hand!

Imagine being at home and going from one room to another. You have just changed your position and orientation. But what has actually changed? We are made up of trillions of cells, which are in turn made from a ridiculous number of molecules. The molecules are in turn made of smaller parts all the way down to electrons, quarks, gluons, and a sea of virtual particles. We are made from an unbelievable number of "things", and all these tiny parts of us have a location that changes as we go about our days. Even the idea of a "location" becomes fuzzy at the smallest scales, with quantum particles having a probability of being somewhere rather than a defined location. These smallest parts of us also behave like particles and waves, which further muddies our general understanding of a position.

The 3D models created by artists are also made from smaller things, but the story is not as complicated. The surface of each model is made up of lots of small triangles. Each triangle corner is called a vertex position, and I like to think of that as being the smallest building block of a model (along with normals and texture coordinates). So, when you are rotating and moving models you are actually manipulating every single triangle that makes up the mesh. These vertex positions can also be scaled to make the model bigger or smaller.

We tend to write positions as a vector (x, y, z), with the three numbers corresponding to the location along the x, y, and z-axes. This can be easily confused with a direction (x, y, z), but we want to treat vertex positions and vertex normal directions differently. To avoid future pitfalls, add one more number to the list called "w" or the homogeneous coordinate if you like to be fancy. When w = 1 it signifies a position and when w = 0 we mean a direction. I know it sounds arbitrary, but for now think of it as an on/off switch. When w = 1 translations are allowed and when w = 0 the translation matrix is disabled. This helps us treat vertex positions and vertex normal directions differently as we move from model to world space.

Does all this speak of a (x, y, z, w) vector make you think about 4D space? Don't stress about it, I find it impossible to imagine anything past three dimensions. I’ve read that 3D space can be thought of as a slice of 4D space where w = 1. That stops my brain from melting on this topic, as I can visualize 2D space as being a slice of 3D, so it's the same idea but just one dimension up. That is the only somewhat useful thing I have to say about 4D space, so my general advice is not to think about extra dimensions too much. I have found it much more helpful to think about w being an on/off switch for translations or the intersection of three perpendicular planes through the origin. If your w component is 1, you are safely in 3D land. If w = 0, then you are dealing with a direction. If w is any other number, run away! Or even better, divide it out so we get back to a 3D position where w = 1. Ah, I feel better already.

I usually think of just the vertices when I see a model, but the normals are so important to make an object feel real. I always thought normal vectors are all 90 degrees to the surface rendered, so watching Paul Neale describe how normals can be mapped from a high-resolution model to a low poly version really shocked me. It made me realize that normals don't have to be tied to the vertices rendered. Studios often strive to render as much detail as possible at their intended frame rate, so it makes sense that artists would use normals from one model, vertices from another, and then combine them on screen to maximize performance.

I began to understand the importance of normal vectors when I started sitting in Scott's Computer Graphics course. He describes a model of lighting published by Bui Tuong Phong in 1975. The Phong lighting model was a sensation at the time and it's my favorite way to see how normal vectors influence the way we view 3D objects. The model starts with a constant called ambient light. That's the flat color objects have when in shadow as shown below:


Ok, it’s just a dark green circle. Now here’s where the normals come in to make it look three-dimensional. Phong's insight was that the shape's color should be brightest when the normal vector points directly at the light source. As the angle between the normal and light direction becomes bigger, the color becomes darker until eventually becoming black when the angle hits 90 degrees. This gradient of color intensity is called the diffuse light reflection as shown below:


Have I tricked you into thinking the light is located up to the left? I did that by using a cosine curve to have the diffuse color at maximum brightness when the normal and light directions match and then gradually tapering off the color to black as the angle between the vectors approaches 90 degrees. Phong showed this is simply done with a dot product between the normal and light directions.

The third and final component of the Phong lighting model is to consider shiny objects. Try placing your phone on a table with the screen up and switched off. As you walk around the phone, can you see the reflections of the lights above you? It's these reflections that produce small and bright highlights on a shiny object. Phong called this the specular light and it is calculated by determining if the reflected light off a surface is pointing directly at the viewer. The law of reflection states that the angle between the incoming light and the normal vector is equal to the angle between the outgoing reflection vector and the normal vector. If the reflection vector lines up perfectly with the direction from the vertex to the camera, then set the specular light to a maximum value. As the angle between the reflection and viewer directions grows, the specular light should fade to black. Again, this is done using my favorite vector operation - the dot product! The dot product between the reflection and viewer direction gives you the cosine of the angle between them. The cosine curve gradually tapers off to zero as the angle approaches positive or negative 90 degrees, but Phong noticed that specular highlights are much sharper than that. To control the size of the specular spot, Phong raised the cosine curve to an arbitrary value called the shininess constant. Here's the specular light on the ball with a shininess constant of 200:


Hard to see the ball now, eh? Don’t worry, there is one last move in the Phong lighting model. You need to add the ambient, diffuse, and specular colors together to render the final object:


Behold, a beautiful green and shiny ball! Notice that the vertices stayed the same in all the pictures above, but by considering the angle between the light, reflection, and normal directions you can make a 3D object appear like magic.

I like the scale matrix as it reminds me what a matrix really does. For example, say you want a matrix that does nothing to a vertex. I know it sounds useless, but it's the default matrix whenever you create one in a game engine. In math that would be the equations x = x, y = y and z = z. Nothing ground-breaking. But remember, we can represent a system of equations using matrices, so let's see how it works in this situation:


Who wants to bother with three separate equations when you can summarize it all in one go with a matrix multiplied by a vector! If you stare at my scribbles above long enough, you might glean the method of multiplying a matrix with a vector. Take the first row of the matrix and lift it up like the back of a dump truck. Multiply the elements one by one with the vector components and add them up to find the answer for the x component. Rinse and repeat to find all three components of the final vector. Here's a picture that might help with this process for the matrix above:


Ok, so that's a matrix that does nothing to the vertex. What about making the x coordinate twice as big, the y coordinate three times as big, and the z value four times as big? If I write out those equations, you will see the scale matrix emerge:


Notice we only need a 3x3 matrix (three rows and three columns) to represent a scale along the three axes. But a translation is handled by a 4x4 matrix. It's so convenient to combine transformations together by multiplying them that we tend to write the scale as a 4x4 matrix so that we have the option to combine with translation to build the model matrix. We know that the scale transformation only affects x, y, and z, but leaves the 4th component w alone. If you write out these four equations, you will see the 4x4 scale matrix appear:


It might seem like a waste holding so many zeroes in the 4x4 scale matrix, but it really helps as we move along the rendering pipeline and have to combine with other types of transformations.

How are you reading this sentence? Did you have to move your phone screen towards you or sit yourself in front of a laptop? Somehow these words came close enough to your eyeballs so you could decipher them. That needed a change in position, and we call that a translation!

It's amazing how much of life is moving from one location to another. I am always grateful when I see my students in class. It is very tempting to stay home and play video games, but they found the motivation to change position (to get to my classroom on time) and listen to me talk about math and physics.

The Cartesian system for placing points in 3D space is super handy. We have the x-axis going from left to right, the y-axis going from down to up, and finally the z-axis going from away to closer to you. You can place an object in space by giving it just three numbers - the x, y, z coordinates. Want to move a bit to the right? Add a number to the x coordinate. Want to move down a bit? Subtract a number from the y coordinate. This all feels very natural since the days we were taught the number line, where adding or subtracting moves you along the line.

Things get a bit more complicated when you start thinking about directions. Try pointing somewhere. You can think of that being along the x, y, and/or z directions depending on the direction. Hold on, those are the same three numbers we used to denote position! The direction "up" is (0, 1, 0) and the position one unit along y from the origin is also (0, 1, 0). Can you see where confusion lies ahead?

One way out of this problem of telling the difference between a position and a direction is to branch out from adding/subtracting numbers and using matrix multiplication. I know, it sounds like a huge hassle to talk about matrices when we already have such a great intuition for changing position - but stick with me, it will be worthwhile. Say we want to move 1 along x, 2 along y, and 3 along z. You can encode that into a translation matrix multiplied by a position vector like this:


How do you multiply a matrix by a vector you ask? Grab the first row of the matrix and multiply each element one-by one with the rows in the vector, then add them all up to get the top row of the answer. Rinse and repeat to get all 4 elements of the final answer.

Notice that this translation of (1, 2, 3) works when we add one more component to the position (x, y, z). That number 1 at the bottom of the vector is called the "w component" and an easy way to think about it (for now) is using a 1 allows translations. If that last component w = 0, then translations are switched off like this:


I know it sounds over the top to jump into 4D space to do something as simple as moving a position. Hang in there, we are just getting you prepped for the wild ride that is the rendering pipeline!

We are all spinning. The earth revolves about its axis once a day, our planet orbits the sun once a year, and our star orbits the supermassive black hole in the middle of our galaxy once every 250 million years. That's the big stuff, but even the smallest bits of matter seem to be spinning too. If you zoom in close enough, you'll find that we are made of atoms, that are in turn made up of electrons, quarks, and gluons. These tiny quantum particles have a property called "spin" which gives them something called an angular momentum. Quantum spin is very different to what we experience in our lives as only certain values are allowed and it's a property of things so tiny that they might not have an actual size at all. How can an electron spin if it's a point particle with no spatial dimension? In fact, if the electron was a ball of spinning charge it would need to be spinning faster than light itself. But the angular momentum of the electron can be precisely measured and is at the heart of quantum mechanics.

Another weird thing about particle spin is that the axis of rotation is always about the axis measured. Try measuring the spin of an electron about the x axis and you will find the result is always around x or negative x. Switch over to a measurement along the y axis and then you will see the axis of rotation is around y or negative y. Guess what happens if you look at the same electron along the z axis? The spin is now about z or negative z. This is very different to the spin of everyday objects where the axis of rotation doesn't change based on how you look at it.

If your brain hasn't fried yet, consider that you can't stop an electron's spin. It always has a specific value no matter what you do to the particle. The spin of a quantum particle is a fundamental quantity, like mass and charge, so it's always there along for the ride. Again, this is drastically different to how things behave in our regular lives. You can have a ball sitting on your table with no spin at all. You can decide to spin it about any axes you like. If you know the angle and axis of rotation, you can rotate anything in a computer simulation just like it would in our day-to-day lives. Things just get very strange when you look closely.

I love quaternions. They are cute little mathematical creatures that only have one job in life. They rotate! Compared to matrices that can do all sorts of things, it is nice to have a mathematical tool designed to do just one thing. It's like having the perfect screwdriver for the job at hand and not hammering nails with it.

Scott loves scaring people by saying quaternions live on a four dimensional hypersphere. I have never found satisfaction pondering four dimensions, that part of my brain should just have the label "Here be dragons". Maybe that's why so many people are terrified of quaternions? Turns out there is a different way to think about quaternions that I find much more appealing. What if quaternions are just lines? Lines that you rotate about. That's it! No foolhardy excursions to 4D land needed, we can rest our weary minds.

The quaternion i is the line along the x-axis. It rotates things 180 degrees about the x-axis. Nice! How about j and k? They too are lines that rotate things 180 degrees about the y and z axis respectively. How can I be so sure of this? Well, my eyes were opened by the Game Developer Conference talks given by Hamish Todd in 2024 (links in the additional resources section), and I've been digging into geometric algebra ever since. The speaker introduces the idea of three planes through the origin that reflect things. If you give the planes the names $e_1$, $e_2$, and $e_3$ for the planes with normals along x, y, and z respectively you can start doing some interesting math with them. For example, if you reflect twice in a mirror you end up back where you started. That means $e_1^2 = e_2^2 = e_3^2 = 1$. Also, if you reflect through two of these mirrors in succession, you actually rotate the object by 180 degrees about the third axis. For example $e_2*e_1$ rotates 180 degrees about the z axis as shown in the picture below:


Hold on, that sounds like the quaternion k! Guess what, it is identical! Look at that, a quaternion pops out and all we had to do is think about mirrors, not the mind-bending 4th dimension. I prefer to go with mirrors every time!

The model matrix is made by multiplying the scale, rotation, and translation matrices together. The odd thing is that the order of multiplication matters. For example, say you have a vertex position at the origin. If you rotate that 180 degrees about the z axis and then translate by 1 unit to the right, you end up 1 unit to the right. But if you do the whole process again, but start with translating 1 unit to the right, then rotating 180 degrees about z, you end up at a position 1 unit to the left, as shown in my scribbles below:


The fact that it matters if you rotate then translate versus the other way around is embedded into the mathematics of multiplying matrices. The translate matrix T multiplied with the rotate matrix R gives you a different answer than multiplying them the other way as R * T. This is very different to what we are used to with arithmetic where 3 * 5 = 5 * 3 = 15 and in algebra where x * y = y * x. The question of whether the order of multiplication matters is referred to more succinctly as whether they "commute". My old physics professor Jon Butterworth wrote in his book Atom Land that if matrices A and B don't commute "This doesn't mean that A and B work from home or live over the shop." It specifically means that A * B is not the same as B * A. This distinction is exactly what we see when swapping the order of transformations in real life and plays out perfectly when changing the order of multiplication with matrices.

The order of multiplication isn't just important for 3D simulations, it's built into the very laws of quantum mechanics. When the legendary physicist Paul Dirac was thinking about electrons moving close to the speed of light in 1928, he was faced with an equation where A * B had to equal to -B * A. He turned to matrices, where the order of multiplication matters and he could rely on them not commuting. His equation matched experimental observations to a stunning degree and even predicted the existence of antimatter a few years before the discovery of the positron. It turns out that "commuting or non-commuting" isn't just a question about how you get to work, it's also how the universe works.

World space is where the action happens. All those models that your artist has created are finally together in one scene with a camera and lights. We only have one world, planet Earth, but you can imagine swapping worlds in a video game when you get to the next level, and each scene would have its own set of models, lights and camera setup. Things are happening in world space, objects can have velocity, animations and all sorts of movements. With one origin location and reference frame for all the objects in the world, it is easy to compare distances between models and have them interact with each other.

To bring a model’s vertices into world space we need one thing, the model matrix! In fact, the model matrix is actually built out of three separate matrices that scale, rotate and translate the model. It’s not so easy for the model’s normals as we don’t want to change their directions, so we need to switch off translations for them and handle any pesky non-uniform scales. The standard way of doing that is the inverse transpose of the model matrix cast down from a 4x4 to a 3x3 matrix. Maybe read that previous sentence again a few times, it is not intuitive. The inverse and the transpose are the same thing for the rotation matrix, so the process keeps rotations intact. The inverse transpose causes the scale on the normal vectors to go in the opposite direction to the vertices. Here’s a picture of what I mean:


Notice that as the vertices on the ball stretch left, the normals point more to the right. And vice versa.

Finally, knocking the model matrix down from a 4x4 to a 3x3 removes any translations from the model matrix. That means our normal direction won’t be moved.

If that all sounds very annoying, then just ensure your model matrix only performs a uniform scale along all three axes. Then turning the normal into a 4D vector with w = 0 will be enough to remove any translations. Just remember to normalize the vector when you are done.

Sometimes you arrive at World space from Camera space. I do that often when figuring out where the mouse has been clicked in Pixel space and working out where that is in World space. In that case, the view matrix is handy! That takes you from World space to Camera space, so using the inverse of the view matrix will do the trick to go the other way. Apply that to your position in Camera space, and bingo you are in World space!

Cameras are easy to overlook in games. When the camera behaves just as you expect, nobody notices them. It's as if they are invisible to the player until there is a problem. I remember being blown away when I first played Super Mario 64 in 1996 as it was the first Mario game set in 3D. The game is truly amazing and I don't remember being fussed about the camera back then. I played the game again recently, and the first thing I noticed was the camera! It's tricky to line up the perfect jump and there isn't as much freedom to move the camera where I want. I have been spoiled with the decades of iteration on camera systems since the 1990s. I even noticed the game has a character, Lakitu, flying on a cloud dangling a camera towards Mario in the opening cut-scene. It reminded me how new the concept of a 3D virtual camera was at the time as the makers of Super Mario 64 had given the players a reason for the camera pointing at Mario. Lakitu was in the in-game camera operator! It's funny to look at now as we just take it for granted that there is a camera looking into the game world.


Playing 3D games from the 1990s and 2000s shows how tied the camera is to the controls. I remember playing a game where I would push the thumbstick forward to exit out of a tunnel, but then the camera would flip to a view of my character emerging from the gloom. As I continued pushing forward on the thumbstick, I would go back into the tunnel again! Cameras are so important for games that they are included in the 3 Cs of game design - Character, Camera and Controls. It breaks your immersion in a game if you miss a jump because the camera didn't line up in a helpful way, so the feel of a game is closely tied to how it is viewed.

Modern 3D games can have a substantial number of camera options. I counted over 10 different camera views for one of my favorite games, EA FC. The experience of the game is very different if you are zoomed out and playing tactically versus an over-the-shoulder camera view where you feel the intensity of barging past defenders to score a goal. I actually feel more stressed when zoomed in, so the location and direction of the camera influences my feelings directly.



I recently finished the game Cyberpunk 2077, and one of my favorite parts of the game is driving around Night City. I tend to change the camera view so that I can see more of my surroundings and avoid bumping into other cars. But if I want to feel immersed in the virtual world, I change the view to be inside the car. Even though it is the same game, my playstyle changes based on the camera.



With all the camera options we have it's important to change the view presented to the player in a smooth way. If the orientation of the camera is represented by a quaternion, we can smoothly interpolate between views using an operation called Spherical Linear Interpolation (SLERP). In a similar way, the position of the camera can be moved between positions smoothly using a formula called Linear Interpolation (LERP). Building the view matrix using the position and orientation of the camera every frame allows gameplay programmers to ensure players don't get confused by rapid changes in camera motion.

An orbit camera is used often in third-person views, just like Lakitu floating around Mario on a cloud. The tricky thing with orbiting the camera around a character is that the rotation matrix or quaternion only rotates around the origin. To rotate about any other position, you need to pretend the target object is at the origin. Do that by translating the camera's position by the negative of the object's position. Then rotate the camera position using the change in rotation. Finally translate the camera's position back using the target's position vector. I've given the code fragment for this operation in the "Code" segment of this site if you'd like to take a look. Video games don't just stop there with orbit cameras. What if the player orbits the camera so that it goes through a wall or the ground? Gameplay programmers typically move the camera closer to the main character so that the view doesn't clip through geometry and obstruct the player's view or they restrict the rotations allowed.

Next time you play a 3D game, try messing around with the camera system. What motions are allowed, can you toggle between views and how does the camera transition between cut-scenes and playable segments. Once you start noticing the camera you will appreciate all the work the game industry has done since the 1990s to make them feel invisible.

As Scott likes to remind me, it's all relative. Do we want to move the camera, or should we just move the world? As we prepare our scene to be displayed on screen, it is useful to have the camera at the origin location (0, 0, 0) and to be looking along a certain direction. That makes the later operations such as ignoring objects out of the camera's view and the illusion of perspective easier to handle mathematically.

We use the view matrix to jump from World space to Camera space, and all it does is translate and rotate. We translate the world so that the camera is at the origin and rotate the world so the camera is looking down the -z axis. There is no scale, so the objects retain their size. That means World space and Camera space are very similar, just a shift in reference frame.

I do all my physics stuff in World space, but I do listen to Scott sometimes - Camera space is handy too. If I am throwing an object based on where the camera is looking, why not just launch it along the -z axis? That would be a direction in Camera space, so I would just need to convert that over to World space using the inverse view matrix. Then I can happily continue with my physics calculations.

If you have a position in Normalized Device Coordinate (NDC) space and want to come over here to Camera space, you need a different approach. The NDC cube is very different to Camera space. Objects near the front clipping plane are huge and things towards the back are tiny to provide perspective. The origin is in the middle of the box, and somebody decided it should use the left-handed coordinate system. To convert all this to Camera space (which is right-handed for us) you would need to use the inverse projection matrix followed by a perspective divide. That will put the camera back at the origin looking along the -z axis and undo the perspective scaling. That makes Scott happy again!

The projection matrix is hard to describe succinctly as it does so many things. To demonstrate that, let's start with the matrices we've already seen in this series. The translation matrix moves positions and requires a displacement. The rotation matrix rotates things and requires the axis and angle. The scale matrix makes things bigger or smaller and requires the scale factor along the three axes. Ok, so far so good. All those matrices could be explained in a single sentence each. Let's try the topic of this video. The perspective projection matrix defines regions of geometry to be discarded by the graphics card and provides a handle on perspective. The matrix requires the field of view angle along y, the aspect ratio of the rendered window, and the z locations of the near and far clipping planes. Wow, that got complicated fast! Let's go over it slowly.

Ok, what do I mean by defining a region of geometry to be discarded? Up until this point in the rendering pipeline, we have the whole world to play with. In world space you can put models wherever you please as you design complicated levels and place your camera in the scene. Camera space is just like world space, just that the camera is at the origin looking down the -z axis. The projection matrix is our first consideration of what this might look like on a flat screen like the one you are looking at right now. When you take a group photo of your friends or family you might ask them to squeeze together so they can all fit in the shot. The projection matrix performs a similar job. It determines what models will be in the frame when we take a photo with the virtual camera.

The region of space the camera can see up and down comes directly from the field of view angle along y. For example, if the field of view along y is 90 degrees, then there is a top boundary plane at 45 degrees from the middle plane and a bottom boundary 45 degrees below centre. If you remember SOH, CAH, TOA from high school, the tan of an angle gives you the ratio between the opposite and adjacent sides of a right triangle. When looking down the negative z direction, the opposite side of our right triangle is the change in y and the adjacent side is the change in z. Hey, the ratio of the opposite and adjacent sides sounds a lot like a slope of a line which is defined by rise over run! In our case the tan of half the field of view angle along y returns the slope of the top boundary wall which rises upwards and the same function with a minus sign gives the slope of the bottom boundary wall that falls downwards. That sets up our bounds in camera space to be -tan(field of view along y / 2) <= y/z <= tan(field of view along y / 2).


Ok, that's the top and bottom boundary walls done. How about the side ones? This is where the aspect ratio comes in. I'm typing on a laptop with a screen resolution of 2560 x 1600 pixels. The aspect ratio is the number of pixels across divided by the number of pixels vertically, which gives my screen an aspect ratio of 1.6. That means I have 1.6 times more pixels across than vertically. Seeing as we have the two boundary walls that rise and fall, we can use the aspect ratio to set the bounds horizontally in camera space as -tan(field of view along y / 2) * aspect ratio <= x/z <= tan(field of view along y / 2) * aspect ratio.

We have two more planes to set up, but these are the easiest. Have you ever taken a photo with your finger over the lens by accident? Wouldn't it be nice to ignore anything too close to the camera. Well, we have that set up too in the projection matrix! In camera space we are looking down the negative z direction, so we just need to set a plane that cuts the z-axis close to the camera. Ignore anything that is closer to the camera than the near plane. In fact, it would be nice to have one more plane far away from the camera, so we don't have to render those tiny little details far away. These two planes are perpendicular to the z-axis, so there is no slope to worry about, just flat planes defined by their z positions. We give the near plane a z value called z_near and the far plane a z value called z_far. Then the boundaries along z in camera space can be expressed as z_near <= -z <= z_far. We are looking along the -z direction but typically z_near and z_far are given as positive values.


So, there we go, the six boundary tests corresponding to the planes of the viewing frustum (left, right, up, down, near, and far). But wait, there’s more! The projection matrix is not done yet, it also encodes the illusion of perspective. Remember we are looking down the -z axis in camera space. Vertices with a large -z value should look smaller than things much closer with small -z values. Somebody came up with the idea to set the w component to -z. I am not making this up! It's in preparation for the next move called the perspective divide, where you divide each component of the vertex position by w. If you divide a position by a large number, it scales it down, but dividing by a small number scales it up. That means objects closer to the camera will appear big and geometry far away will be shrunk. Don't worry about the z value, the projection matrix takes care of that, so it gets restricted to a range of -1 to +1 after dividing by the w value.

Multiplying the vertices by the projection matrix takes us from camera space to clip space. I don't tend to think of clip space often, as it happens on the hardware without me noticing. We don't want to render any geometry outside our viewing frustum and that’s efficiently done on the GPU by testing the vertices against their w values before the perspective divide operation. In OpenGL, a triangle is kept for rendering if all three corner positions have an x, y, and z value that are all larger or equal to -w and less than or equal to w. If a triangle has one or two vertices that fail this test, the triangle is "clipped" and new vertices are generated at the clip boundary. If all the vertices fail the test, the triangle is discarded from memory. It's a good rule in life to skip useless work, and that's exactly what the GPU does to speed up rendering beautiful art to screen.

Do parallel lines ever meet? When you are driving along an empty and straight stretch of a highway, it looks like the sides of the road might meet if you could look far enough. In fact they do meet, just infinitely far away. That might seem like a non-starter, but the idea of a point infinitely far away is just the sort of thing used in geometric algebra. Instead of throwing your arms up and walking away when faced with infinity, it is handy to give it a name. In projective geometric algebra, the point infinitely far away along the x axis is called e032. It's the intersection two planes going through the origin (e3 faces z and e2 faces y) and the plane infinitely far away called e0. Sure, this sounds like useless jargon, but the math maps exactly with a direction vector pointing to the right (1, 0, 0, 0), even down to the detail of w = 0 for a direction. It brings to mind that when you point to the right along the x-axis, it is conceptually the same as a point infinitely far away along x. It's also the reason you never do a perspective divide operation on a direction, as dividing x, y, z by w = 0 can't possibly convert a direction into a position in 3D space.

The standard way to write down a position is with the w component equal to one. The perspective projection matrix changes that dramatically. It sets the w component to be the -z value and prepares the actual z component for what's coming up next. I know this sounds crazy, but it means w is large for objects far from the camera, and small for things up close. So when you divide all the vector components by w, you end up with x and y being much smaller for objects in the distance and bigger for close to the camera. The z component is constrained between the values -1 and 1 to fit the normalized device coordinate box, and w turns back into one. Conceptually it means a position with a large w value such as (1, 2, 3, 10) is the same as the scaled down position (0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 1). A position with a small w value such as (1, 2, 0.5, 0.5) is the same as the scaled up position (2, 4, 1, 1). If I write that out in a general way, the position (x * w, y * w, z * w, w) for any non-zero w value, is the same as the position (x, y, z, 1) in our familiar 3D space. It's all just a matter of perspective.

A student brought in an NES console with a portable CRT television to my class this semester. He had bought them at a garage sale and was very excited to play some vintage gaming during our break. As he was smacking the TV to get it working, I was reminded that monitors looked like boxes when I was young. Monitors are light and thin nowadays, but they used to be quite heavy and would take up a fair amount of space. Whilst I watched my student play Super Mario Bros., it struck me that it was a nice visual of Normalized Device Coordinate space. His CRT monitor looked like the NDC box which leads us to the final stage of the rendering pipeline with Mario on the screen.

Of course, we shouldn't get too carried away with analogies. The NDC box is actually tiny, being a cube with side lengths of 2 units. It contains all the models that are to be rendered on the screen. I asked our brilliant student artist, Cassidy, to make an NDC box for our video, and it was a delight to physically hold the space I only deal with mathematically. But I do need to remember that the models in NDC space are distorted in size by the aspect ratio of the screen. Eventually we stretch out the box by half the screen width along x and half the screen height along y, so the screen resolution plays a crucial role in NDC space.

When you are planning out a 3D game, you place your models and lights in the world and set up the camera position and orientation. But the player does not see the actual camera, they only see what the camera would see. Anything outside of the camera's view is not rendered, and models closer to the camera seem much bigger than things in the distance. This illusion of a viewing volume and perspective is all set up when you get to NDC space from camera space via the projection matrix and perspective divide. What you see in the NDC box is very similar to what you want on screen, you just have to squint and give it a smack using something called the viewport matrix.

Our universe is expanding. Every galaxy outside of our local group is speeding away from us at an accelerated rate. In fact, every galaxy in the universe is in a similar predicament. It's like all the galaxies are dots on a balloon, and those dots all move away from each other as the balloon is inflated. The viewport matrix might not be as exciting as dark energy, but it does make the universe of our game dramatically bigger.

Our entire game, at this point in our series, sits in a tiny box called normalized device coordinate (NDC) space. In the OpenGL graphics library, this is a cube with side lengths of 2 units. We need to make this much bigger to get to pixel space and have something rendered to screen. I'm typing on a laptop that has a screen resolution of 2560 x 1600. That means the NDC box needs to be stretched out to fit 2560 pixels across and 1600 pixels vertically. As the box already started out with a width and height of 2, that gives us a scale of 2560/2=1280 along x and 1600/2=800 along y. Don't worry about this stretching out your models in weird ways, the aspect ratio of the screen is already baked into NDC space.

The viewport matrix also does other things to match the conventions. In NDC space, y points up (for OpenGL) and the position (0, 0, 0) is in the centre of the cube. But in pixel space, y points down and the position (0, 0) is in the top left corner of the screen. Scott handles this in code by first flipping the sign on the y coordinate then scaling and translating the positions by half the screen width along x and half the screen height along y. He also constrains the z values to be between 0 and 1 to fit the usual conventions for GPU cards.

The expansion of the NDC box stops at the screen’s pixel resolution, but it's an open question on whether the universe itself will expand forever. Stay tuned!

Reach out and touch your screen. This is pixel space! I'm typing on my laptop with a screen resolution of 2560 x 1600. That means there are 2560 pixels across and 1600 pixels going up and down. That's over 4 million tiny pixels covering my screen. Looking up the specs online, my screen has 188 pixels per inch. Converting that over to millimetres, each pixel on my screen is about 0.1 mm in length. That's tiny! No wonder I can't see the individual pixels by eye.

The word pixel comes from the word "picture" and "element" smooshed together in an interesting way. But just as chemical elements are made from smaller objects, so are picture elements. Each pixel on my screen is made up of three subpixels that shine red, green and blue light. As Scott mentioned in the video, our eyeballs contain cone cells that are sensitive to those same three colours. What a coincidence! (not)

I can't make out the pixels, let alone the subpixels, so my brain just sees the combination of red, green and blue as one colour. Each subpixel carries 8 bits of information, which turns out to be 2^8 = 256 levels of red, blue and green individually. By varying the intensity of each subpixel, my screen can show 256^3 = roughly 16.7 million colours! I can't tell maroon from mahogany, so that’s more than enough for me.

Colouring each individual pixel seems like an awful amount of work, but thankfully we have Graphics Processing Units (GPUs) to speed us up tremendously. Programmers can choose the colour of each pixel in a piece of code called a "fragment shader" that runs on the GPU. Take a look at some examples on shadertoy.com to see the possibilities!

Pixel space is surprisingly similar to Normalized Device Coordinate (NDC) space. Sure, the NDC box has a width and height of 2 units, but we just need to stretch that out to fit the number of pixels needed horizontally and vertically. The depth information along z is not shown on the screen but is useful to figure out what should be shown in front of something else. The origin (0, 0) in Pixel space is in the top left corner with y pointing down. Why, you ask? Probably a relic from a bygone era when electrons were fired at CRT TV screens to light them up from behind, starting at the top left corner and scanning across. You can transform a position in NDC space to Pixel space using the viewport matrix which scales the NDC box to fit the screen resolution whilst retaining the z information for depth testing and sticks the origin in the top left corner with y pointing down. Now you can look at your beautiful 3D scene!

If you clicked on the screen and want to figure out what you clicked on, you'll need to hop over from Pixel to NDC space. That just involves the inverse of the viewport matrix. Then you can click or tap at your heart's content.
